rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jaʿfar b. Muḥammad recommends giving one third to the contented and needy petitioner, one third to the destitute poor, and one third to one's family.
rows.anchor: وقال جعفر بن محمد أطعم القانع والمعتر ثلثا، والبائس الفقير ثلثا، وأهلي ثلثا

rows.speaker: ابن المسيب
rows.claim: Ibn al-Musayyab limits the owner to one quarter of the sacrificial animal; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says all these shares are recommendations, not obligations.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن المسيب: ليس لصاحب الهدي منه إلا الربع وهذا كله على جهة الاستحباب لا الفرض قاله ابن عطية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God made sacrificial camels submissive so people can lead, restrain, and slaughter them; without divine subjection, humans could not manage them, as wild camels demonstrate.
rows.anchor: ولولا تسخير الله لم تطق ولم تكن بأعجز من بعض الوحوش

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says Muslims wanted to imitate pagan slaughter, displaying meat around the Kaʿba and splashing its walls with blood as worship; the verse was revealed in response. Ibn ʿAbbās reports something similar.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: أراد المسلمون أن يفعلوا فعل المشركين من الذبح وتشريح اللحم منصوبا حول الكعبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Neither donated meat nor shed blood reaches God's approval; worshippers attain acceptance through sincere intention, piety, lawful offerings, and observance of religious duties, not through abundant sacrifice alone.
rows.anchor: لن يصيب رضا الله اللحوم المتصدق بها ولا الدماء المهراقة بالنحر

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains that the verse's wording is amplified: sacrifice and offerings avail only when their conditions of piety and sincerity are observed.
rows.anchor: فإذا لم يراعوا ذلك لم تغن عنهم التضحية والتقريب، وإن كثر ذلك منهم قاله الزمخشري

rows.speaker: يحيى بن يعمر
rows.claim: Yahya b. Yaʿmar and al-Jaḥdarī read the verb with tāʾ in “taqwa reaches Him.”
rows.anchor: تناله التقوى بالتاء يحيى بن يعمر والجحدري

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd b. ʿAlī reads “their meat and their blood” in the accusative and reads “but taqwa reaches Him” with an initial yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي لحومها ولا دماءها بالنصب ولكن يناله بضم الياء

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the repeated reminder of subjection calls for gratitude for guidance to the religion and pilgrimage rites; takbīr is made to carry the sense and syntax of thanks.
rows.anchor: لتشكروا الله على هدايته إياكم لإعلام دينه ومناسك حجه بأن تكبروا وتهللوا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the good-doers promised glad tidings as those who affirm God's oneness; a report also says the verse was revealed about the four caliphs.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: وهم الموحدون وروي أنها نزلت في الخلفاء الأربعة

none: This segment contains Qurʾān text only, without commentary.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamz means poking or driving with a hand or other means; it also describes a riding goad and verbal assault on people.
rows.anchor: الهمز: النخس والدفع بيد وغيرها، ومنه مهماز الرائض وهمز الناس باللسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Barzakh is an intervening barrier between two distances or things that keeps one from reaching the other.
rows.anchor: البرزخ: الحاجز بين المسافتين. وقيل: الحجاب بين الشيئين يمنع أحدهما أن يصلى إلى الآخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nasab means kinship through birth.
rows.anchor: النسب: القرابة من جهة الولادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lafḥ is the scorching impact of fire's heat; al-Zajjāj says it has a stronger effect than laqīḥ.
rows.anchor: اللفح: إصابة النار الشيء بوهجها وإحراقها. وقال الزجاج: اللفح أشد من اللقيح تأثيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kulūḥ is lips pulling back from the teeth, like a dog's or lion's grimace; another explanation is a frowning, contorted face, with several related word forms.
rows.anchor: الكلوح: تشمر الشفتين عن الأسنان ومنه كلوح كلوح الكلب والأسد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAbath means play or activity with no benefit.
rows.anchor: العبث: اللعب الخالي عن فائدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage follows the disbelievers' refusal to hear evidence and contemplate signs: those who fail to use their faculties to recognize God are like people without those faculties.
rows.anchor: من لم يعمل هذه الأعضاء في ما خلقه الله تعالى وتدبر ما أودعه فيها من الدلائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The one who created the senses, gives life and death, and governs night and day can also resurrect; these faculties serve religious and worldly needs by hearing and seeing signs and reasoning about God's unity and attributes.
rows.anchor: فمن أنشأ هذه الحواس وأنشئت هي له وأحيا وأمات وتصرف في اختلاف الليل والنهار هو قادر على البعث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Little are you grateful” means people give little thanks; the extra māʾ emphasizes the statement, and gratitude entails acknowledging the giver and denying partners.
rows.anchor: قليلا ما تشكرون أي تشكرون قليلا وما زائدة للتأكيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dharʾ means creating and spreading people through the earth; they are gathered to God's judgment, decree, and recompense in the resurrection after worldly dispersal and decay.
rows.anchor: وذرأكم خلقكم وبثكم فيها. وإليه أي وإلى حكمه وقضائه وجزائه تحشرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternation of night and day means each succeeds the other; God alone directs this change and has power over it.
rows.anchor: والاختلاف هنا التعاقب أي يخلف هذا هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reasoning from these acts of power should lead people to affirm God's oneness and deny partners, who can do none of them.
rows.anchor: أفلا تعقلون من هذه تصرفات قدرته وآثار قهره فتوحدونه وتنفون عنه الشركاء والأنداد

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr transmits the third-person reading “yaʿqilūn,” a shift of address.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو في رواية: يعقلون بياء الغيبة على الالتفات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Rather” marks a turn: Meccans and similar people repeat their ancestors' denial of resurrection, although they admit God's ownership of earth and heaven while attributing offspring and partners to Him.
rows.anchor: بل إضراب أي ليس لهم عقل ولا نظر في هذه الآيات بل قالوا والضمير لأهل مكة

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh, al-Ḥasan, al-Jaḥdarī, Naṣr b. ʿĀṣim, Ibn Waththāb, Abū al-Ashhab, and Abū ʿAmr read the second and third replies as nominative “Allāh”; the other seven read “li-llāh.” The first agrees in wording, the second in meaning.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله والحسن والجحدري ونصر بن عاصم وابن وثاب

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Muḥayṣin reads the mīm of “al-ʿaẓīm” with ḍamma as an adjective of “Lord.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن محيصن العظيم برفع الميم نعتا للرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To protect someone from another is the sense of ijārah: God protects whomever He wills, and nobody can protect anyone from Him.
rows.anchor: أي وهو يمنع من يشاء ممن يشاء ولا يمنع أحد منه أحدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their admission “God” does not conflict with “if you know”; the conditional does not deny their knowledge and rhetorically underscores it. Each question ends with a fitting reminder, then the stronger warning of taqwa.
rows.anchor: ولا تعارض بين قوله إن كنتم تعلمون لا ينفي عنهم وبين ما حكى عنهم من قولهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “How are you bewitched?” rebukes them for being confused about monotheism and obedience despite their admissions; magic is a metaphor for putting words and actions in the wrong places.
rows.anchor: أنى بمعنى كيف قرر أنهم مسحورون وسألهم عن الهيئة التي سحروا بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is also read “bal ātaytuhum” with first-person tāʾ, or with an addressee tāʾ; the disbelievers lie about God's having a child or partners and other claims.
rows.anchor: وقرىء بل آتيتهم بتاء المتكلم، وابن أبي إسحاق بتاء الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's denial of a child answers claims that angels are His daughters; denial of another god answers idol worship and may also refute Christians and dualists.
rows.anchor: فنفي الولد تنبيه على من قال: الملائكة بنات الله، ونفي الشريك في الألوهية تنبيه على من قال: الأصنام آلهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If there were several gods, each would isolate its creation and kingdom or overpower the others like worldly kings; the absence of such division proves one God. The omitted conditional is signaled by the preceding denial, as al-Farrāʾ explains.
rows.anchor: ومعنى لذهب أي لا نفرد كل إله بخلقه الذي خلق واستبد به وتميز ملك كل واحد عن ملك الآخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “bimā khalaq,” mā is apparently a relative pronoun, though it may be a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن ما في بما خلق بمعنى الذي وجوز أن تكون مصدرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Glory be to God above what they describe” disavows the claims of offspring and partners; a reading changes the verb to second-person address.
rows.anchor: سبحان الله عما يصفون تنزيه عن الولد والشريك. وقرىء عما تصفون بتاء الخطاب

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: For “ʿālim,” al-Zamakhsharī takes the genitive reading as an adjective of God; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it following the written form. The nominative is read by the remaining listed authorities.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: صفة لله. وقال ابن عطية: اتباع للمكتوبة

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash prefers the genitive for syntactic continuity; Abū ʿAlī treats the nominative as a new clause with an omitted “He is,” while Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers the nominative.
rows.anchor: قال الأخفش: الجر أجود ليكون الكلام من وجه واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fāʾ before “fa-taʿālā” may coordinate the meaning “He knows the unseen and seen, so He is exalted,” or introduce a fresh report, “I say: exalted is He.”
rows.anchor: والفاء في قوله فتعالى عاطفة فالمعنى كأنه قال عالم الغيب والشهادة فتعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unseen is what people do not see, and the witnessed is what they see.
rows.anchor: والغيب ما غاب عن الناس والشهادة ما شاهدوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the accusations of offspring and partners, the Prophet is told to pray not to be among the wrongdoers if their threatened punishment occurs; this expresses servanthood and humility despite his immunity from culpable causes.
rows.anchor: ولكنه أمره أن يدعو بذلك إظهارا للعبودية وتواضعا لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's repeated request for forgiveness after gatherings and Abū Bakr's statement that he was not the best leader illustrate believers' self-effacement; al-Ḥasan says Abū Bakr knew he was best but humbled himself.
rows.anchor: واستغفار رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا قام من مجلسه سبعين مرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating “Lord” before the condition and its consequence intensifies pleading and appeal, since the Lord owns and oversees the servant's interests.
rows.anchor: وجاء الدعاء بلفظ الرب قبل الشرط وقبل: الجزاء مبالغة في الابتهال إلى الله تعالى والتضرع

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Abū ʿAmr al-Jawnī read “tarʾanī” with hamza instead of yāʾ, a weak substitution also found in other forms.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الضحاك وأبو عمر إن الجوني ترئني بالهمز بدل الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God could hasten the promised punishment during the Prophet's life, but deferred it to its appointed term; most say it is worldly punishment, variously identified as Badr, the conquest of Mecca, or the afterlife.
rows.anchor: والجمهور على أن هذا العذاب في الدنيا. فقيل: يوم بدر. وقيل: فتح مكة. وقيل: هو عذاب الآخرة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: The best response to evil is the testimony that there is no god but God; al-Ḥasan instead glosses it as pardon and forbearance, while ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḍaḥḥāk say to greet abusers.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: الصفح والإغضاء. وقال عطاء والضحاك: السلام إذا أفحشوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Māwardī says to repel wrongdoing by admonition; the author prefers the general sense of answering both good and harm with the best conduct, strengthened by the comparative “best.”
rows.anchor: وحكى الماوردي: ادفع بالموعظة المنكر والأجود العموم في الحسنى وفيما يسوء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some call this verse abrogated by the sword verse; the author favors its continued force because accommodation is encouraged unless it compromises religion or honor.
rows.anchor: قيل: وهذه الآية منسوخة بآية السيف. وقيل: هي محكمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We know best what they describe” indicates a truce and concerns their false descriptions of the Prophet.
rows.anchor: نحن أعلم بما يصفون يقتضي أنها آية موادعة

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Satan's hamz means madness according to Ibn Zayd; the apparent command is to seek refuge from satanic presence at all times, while Ibn ʿAbbās specifies during Qurʾān recitation.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: همز الشيطان الجنون، والظاهر أنه أمر بالاستعاذة من حضور الشياطين في كل وقت

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī connects “until death comes” to the disbelievers' continued bad speech, taking the intervening prayer as a parenthetical appeal for divine help against satanic provocation.
rows.anchor: حتى يتعلق بيصفون أي لا يزالون على سوء الذكر إلى هذا الوقت

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya treats ḥattā as an opening particle, possibly marking an endpoint with omitted words; the author objects that even an opening ḥattā retains endpoint force and Ibn ʿAṭiyya leaves the omission unexplained.
rows.anchor: حتى في هذا الموضع حرف ابتداء، ويحتمل أن تكون غاية مجردة بتقدير كلام محذوف

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ says ḥattā marks an endpoint in a sense like coordination; the author's own reconstruction supplies an omitted clause: the Prophet will not be like disbelievers attended by satans until death.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو البقاء حتى غاية في معنى العطف

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayrī says the disbelievers persist in denial despite God's proofs until death brings certainty, sight of the angels, and useless regret.
rows.anchor: وقال القشيري: احتج تعالى عليهم وذكرهم قدرته ثم قال: مصرون على الإنكار

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: The plural in “return me” may reverentially address God as a plural, or the dying person may first appeal to God and then call the punishment angels; Ibn Jurayj gives the latter explanation.
rows.anchor: وإما استغاث أولا بربه وخاطب ملائكة العذاب وقاله ابن جريج

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says one who failed to pay alms and perform pilgrimage asks to return; others object that the verse concerns disbelievers and cite the call to spend in 63:10. Al-Awzāʿī identifies the asker as one who withheld alms.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: من لم يزك ولم يحج سأل الرجعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When death arrives and the person sees it, he asks to return to worldly life.
rows.anchor: وجاء الموت أي حضر وعاينه الإنسان فحينئذ يسأل الرجعة إلى الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith contrasts the believer, who declines return to the home of sorrows and goes on to God, with the disbeliever, who asks to return and do good.
rows.anchor: إذا عاين المؤمن الموت قالت له الملائكة: نرجعك فيقول إلى دار الهموم والأحزان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In what I left” can mean the faith abandoned: the dying person hopes to perform the good he omitted, like someone who says he will build on a foundation, meaning first lay one.
rows.anchor: ومعنى فيما تركت في الإيمان الذي تركته والمعنى لعلي آتي بما تركته من الإيمان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās also interprets what was left behind as wealth.
rows.anchor: وقيل: فيما تركت من المال على ما فسره ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “No” rejects and rules out the request to return; it may be God's rebuke or the dying person's self-reproach, whose repeated words are useless and unanswered.
rows.anchor: كلا كلمة ردع عن طلب الرجعة وإنكار واستبعاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The barzakh is a barrier preventing disbelievers' return until resurrection; it makes return to worldly life wholly hopeless and names the period between death and resurrection metaphorically.
rows.anchor: ومن ورائهم أي الكفار برزخ حاجز بينهم وبين الرجعة إلى وقت البعث

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says kinship disappears at the first trumpet because people die then; this interpretation lessens the horror of the gathering.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس: عند النفخة الأولى يموت الناس فلا يكون بينهم نسب في ذلك الوقت

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd and others place the severing of kinship when people rise from graves: each is preoccupied, ending reliance on and boasting through family ties.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن مسعود وغيره: عند قيام الناس من القبور فلهول المطلع اشتغل كل امرئ بنفسه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says a person most dislikes meeting someone he knows that day, for fear of an unpaid grievance; the passage echoes the flight from relatives in 80:34–36.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة: ليس أحد أبغض إلى الإنسان في ذلك اليوم ممن يعرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that family members do not connect when separated for their allotted reward or punishment; only deeds create their connection.
rows.anchor: وقيل: فلا أنساب أي لا تواصل بينهم حين افتراقهم إلى ما أعد لهم

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh reads “wa-lā yasāʾalūn” with a doubled sīn, assimilating the tāʾ of the underlying “yataṣāʾalūn.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله ولا يساءلون بتشديد السين أدغم التاء في السين إذ أصله يتساءلون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The absence of questions here does not conflict with questions in 37:27 because resurrection has different stages; questions may occur at the second trumpet after their absence at the first.
rows.anchor: ولا تعارض بين انتفاء التساؤل هنا وبين إثباته في قوله وأقبل بعضهم على بعض يتساءلون

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī offers several syntactic analyses for “abiding in Hell,” including a predicate or an apposition related to loss of selves.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري في جهنم خالدون بدل من خسروا أنفسهم ولا محل للبدل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author calls the apposition analysis unusual: it means “settled in Hell,” a rhetorical apposition between equivalent referents because losing oneself leads to Hell; the apparent syntax makes Hell the predicate, not an adjective.
rows.anchor: جعل في جهنم بدلا من خسروا وهذا بدل غريب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The face is singled out because it is the person's most honored and protected part; if fire scorches it, the lesser parts are scorched too, leading into the description of grimacing lips.
rows.anchor: وخص الوجه باللفح لأنه أشرف ما في الإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tirmidhī records that the upper lip contracts to the middle of the head and the lower lip hangs to the navel; he grades the report ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ.
rows.anchor: وفي الترمذي تتقلص شفته العليا حتى تبلغ وسط رأسه

rows.speaker: أبو حيوة
rows.claim: Abū Ḥaywah, Abū Baḥriyya, and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read “kāliḥūn” without the alif.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو حيوة وأبو بحرية وابن أبي عبلة كلحون بغير ألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God questions the condemned through whichever angels He wills; “My signs” means the Qurʾān.
rows.anchor: يقول الله لهم على لسان من يشاء من ملائكته ألم تكن آياتي وهي القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their “misery overcame us” means it took and mastered them; misery ordinarily means an evil outcome, but al-Jubbāʾī says it means desire and indulgence because these cause misery, while another view calls it what was decreed and foreknown.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الشقوة الهوى وقضاء اللذات لأن ذلك يؤدي إلى الشقوة

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: Several authorities read “shaqāwatunā” with alif in the pattern of saʿāda; Qatāda and al-Ḥasan also have a kasra variant, while the majority use the common Hijazi form with a still qāf.
rows.anchor: والمفضل عن عاصم وأبان والزعفراني وابن مقسم

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ cites Abū Tharwān's verse as poetic evidence for the hardship reading of “shaqāwatunā.”
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: أنشدني أبو ثروان وكان فصيحا

rows.speaker: شبل
rows.claim: Shibl reads “shaqwatunā” with fatḥa on the shīn and a still qāf.
rows.anchor: وقرأ شبل في اختياره بفتح الشين وسكون القاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We were a misguided people” means they had strayed from guidance; their confession leads into a plea for release from Hell, promising not to return to disbelief and idolatry.
rows.anchor: وكنا قوما ضالين أي عن الهدى، ثم تدرجوا من الإقرار إلى الرغبة والتضرع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If returned, they would wrong themselves again by renewed transgression after first wronging themselves and then receiving reprieve.
rows.anchor: فإنا ظالمون أي متجاوزو الحد في العدوان حيث ظلمنا أنفسنا أولا ثم سومحنا

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī transmits a long dialogue among the disbelievers, Mālik, and God ending in Hell closing and the condemned barking at one another; Ibn ʿAṭiyya abridges it as unsound in transmission but sound in meaning.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: واختصرت ذلك الحديث لعدم صحته، لكن معناه صحيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Ikhsāʾū” means to be humiliated and driven away as dogs are rebuked; the verb may be transitive or intransitive.
rows.anchor: ومعنى اخسؤا أي ذلوا فيها وانزجروا كما تنزجر الكلاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Do not speak to Me” forbids asking for relief or a reduction; some say it is their last speech, after which only groaning and doglike howling remain.
rows.anchor: ولا تكلمون أي في رفع العذاب أو تخفيفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believing servants are the vulnerable believers; the rebuke addresses Meccan disbelievers who mocked Ṣuhayb, ʿAmmār, and Bilāl, and applies generally across eras.
rows.anchor: ونزلت في كفار قريش مع صهيب وعمار وبلال ونظرائهم، ثم هي عامة

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy and Hārūn al-ʿAtakī read the opening of “annahu kāna” with fatḥa, meaning “because”; the majority read kasra, with the pronoun of the matter omitted under the open hamza.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبي وهارون العتكي أنه بفتح الهمزة أي لأنه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says the kasra in “sukhriyyan” forms an intensified verbal noun of mockery; Khalīl, Abū Zayd, and Sībawayh take it as ridicule, while Abū ʿUbayda, al-Kisāʾī, and al-Farrāʾ distinguish ḍamma for service from kasra for mockery.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة والكسائي والفراء: ضم السين من السخرة والاستخدام والكسر من السخر وهو الاستهزاء

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yūnus says ḍamma is required when service is meant, while either ḍamma or kasra may mean mockery; al-Aʿshā's line attests the ridicule sense.
rows.anchor: وقال يونس: إذا أريد التخديم فضم السين لا غير، وإذا أريد الهزء فالضم والكسر

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya records that ʿAbd Allāh's readers and Ibn Abī Isḥāq and al-Aʿraj use ḍamma throughout, while al-Ḥasan and Abū ʿAmr use kasra except in al-Zukhruf; Abū ʿAlī prefers kasra here because the context says they laughed.
rows.anchor: وكان قد قال عن أبي علي يعني الفارسي أن قراءة كسر السين أوجه لأنه بمعنى الاستهزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya's claim of consensus on ḍamma in al-Zukhruf is inaccurate: Ibn Muḥayṣin and Ibn Muslim read kasra there.
rows.anchor: وليس ما ذكره من إجماع القراء على ضم السين في الزخرف صحيحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers were mocked and distracted the mockers from remembering God; forgetfulness is attributed to the disbelievers because their ridicule caused it.
rows.anchor: فاتخذتموهم سخريا أي هزأة تهزؤون منهم حتى أنسوكم ذكري

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: Zayd b. ʿAlī, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Khārija from Nāfiʿ read “innahum hum” with kasra; the other seven read fatḥa.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي وحمزة والكسائي وخارجة عن نافع إنهم هم بكسر الهمزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second object of “I rewarded them” is omitted, perhaps Paradise or God's approval; al-Zamakhsharī takes it as “their victory,” while the author prefers a causal reading, “because they are the successful.”
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه تعليل أي جزيتهم لأنهم، والكسر هو على الاستئناف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The successful are those rescued from ruin into bliss.
rows.anchor: والفائزون الناجون من هلكة إلى نعمة

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Ibn Kathīr read “qul kam” as an imperative addressed to an angel or another inhabitant of Hell; the remaining readers have “qāla,” spoken by God or an assigned angel.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي وابن كثير قل كم والمخاطب ملك يسألهم أو بعض أهل النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about years is a demand that fixes them to an answer; most read “ʿadada sinīn” as a construct, with “how many” measuring time and “number” specifying it. A reading with indefinite “ʿadadan” allows other parses, but “labithtum” as “you counted” is remote.
rows.anchor: سألهم سؤال توقيف على المدة. وقرأ الجمهور عدد سنين على الإضافة

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī and al-Zamakhsharī take their stay on earth as worldly life; terror makes them forget it and answer uncertainly “a day or part of a day,” as Ibn ʿAbbās explains.
rows.anchor: يعني في الحياة الدنيا قاله الطبري وتبعه الزمخشري

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Most interpreters instead understand “on earth” as the time dead in the grave; Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers this because they denied resurrection and the passage ends by saying they would not return to God.
rows.anchor: وهذا قول جمهور المتأولين. قال ابن عطية: وهذا هو الأصوب

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid identifies the counters as angels who record people's deeds and count their hours; Qatāda says they are accountants, while the author allows anyone who can count.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: العادين الملائكة أي هم الذين يحفظون أعمال بني آدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent sense includes angels or others who can count, since sleepers and the dead cannot track time. Al-Zamakhsharī says torment makes the interval feel slight and leaves them unable to calculate or explain it.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنهم من يتصف بهذه الصفة ملائكة أو غيرهم لأن النائم والميت لا يعد

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Ḥasan and al-Kisāʾī transmit a light-dāl reading meaning wrongdoers; another form with long yāʾ means ancient people or long-lived elders, who would consider the period short too.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن والكسائي في رواية العادين بتخفيف الدال أي الظلمة

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: The two Kūfan readers make “qul in labithtum” an imperative; the remaining seven read “in” as negation: they stayed only a little compared with their torment, or because whatever is coming is near if the grave is meant.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأخوان قل إن لبثتم على الأمر، وباقي السبعة وإن نافية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In vain” can describe their state or give the purpose; humans were created for obligation and worship, not futile play. The phrase about not returning is coordinated with “that we created you.”
rows.anchor: وانتصب عبثا على الحال أي عابثين أو على أنه مفعول من أجله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two Kūfans read “lā tarjiʿūn” actively and the others passively; al-Zamakhsharī also parses “and that you will not return” as a purpose of futility.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأخوان لا ترجعون مبنيا للفاعل، وباقي السبعة مبنيا للمفعول

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī offers “for play” and “so that you would not be returned” as purpose complements of “in vain.”
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: يجوز أن يكون على عبثا أي للعبث ولترككم غير مرجوعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is exalted above spouse, child, partner, futility, and every imperfection; He is the true King, and “the Generous” describes the Throne because blessings descend from it or by its relation to the Most Generous.
rows.anchor: فتعالى الله أي تعاظم وتنزه عن الصاحبة والولد والشريك والعبث وجميع النقائص

rows.speaker: أبان بن تغلب
rows.claim: Abān b. Taghlib, Ibn Muḥayṣin, Abū Jaʿfar, and Ismāʿīl from Ibn Kathīr read “al-karīm” in the nominative, as an adjective of the Lord or Throne in an added expression of praise.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبان بن تغلب وابن محيصن وأبو جعفر وإسماعيل عن ابن كثير الكريم بالرفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “With no proof” is a reinforcing, always-true attribute, not an exception implying that another god might have proof; it may be parenthetical. Making it the conditional answer would improperly omit the required fāʾ.
rows.anchor: ولا برهان له به صفة لازمة لا للاحتراز من أن يكون ثم آخر يقوم عليه برهان

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Ḥasan and Qatāda read the opening of “annahu lā yufliḥ” with fatḥa, construing it as a predicate and replacing the pronoun with “the disbelievers” according to the meaning of “whoever”; the majority read kasra as a new clause.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وقتادة أنه لا يفلح بفتح الهمزة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Ḥasan also reads “yufliḥ” with fatḥa on both fāʾ and lām.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن يفلح بفتح الفاء واللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah opens by saying believers prosper and closes by saying disbelievers do not prosper, deliberately contrasting its opening and ending.
rows.anchor: وافتتح السورة بقوله قد أفلح المؤمنون وأورد في خاتمتها إنه لا يفلح الكافرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Messenger is told to ask forgiveness and mercy; Ibn Muḥayṣin reads “rabb” with a ḍamma on its bāʾ.
rows.anchor: ثم أمر رسوله عليه السلام بأن يدعو بالغفران والرحمة. وقرأ ابن محيصن رب بضم الباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the example of believer and disbeliever, the passage adduces signs of divine power and oneness; “whoever is in the earth” apparently means obedient humans and jinn, though another reading makes it all beings, with rational form covering nonrational beings.
rows.anchor: والظاهر حمل التسبيح على حقيقته وتخصيص من في قوله ومن في الأرض بالمطيع لله تعالى من الثقلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternative explanations take glorification as these beings' testimony that God is free of imperfection and possesses perfection, or as magnification expressed by prayer for rational creatures and indication for others; Sufyān says each thing glorifies by obedience and submission.
rows.anchor: وقال سفيان: تسبيح كل شيء بطاعته وانقياده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Birds are singled out because in flight they spread their wings between heaven and earth, outside the ordinary grouping of beings in either realm.
rows.anchor: وإنما خص الطير بالذكر لأنها تكون بين السماء والأرض إذا طارت

rows.speaker: الأعرج
rows.claim: Most read “al-ṭayr” nominative with “whoever” and “ṣāffāt” accusative as a state; al-Aʿraj reads the bird as an accusative comitative object, while other named readers raise both as subject and predicate.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعرج والطير بالنصب على أنه مفعول معه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Most say birds truly glorify God; al-Zamakhsharī says God may inspire their prayer just as He inspires their intricate skills, while al-Ḥasan and others take their wise design as figuratively calling people to glorify.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: ولا يبعد أن يلهم الله الطير دعاءه وتسبيحه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan and al-Zajjāj take the subject of “knows” and the possessors of prayer and glorification as each creature; another view assigns “knows” to each and prayer and glorification to God as creator and guide.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: الضمير في علم وفي صلاته وتسبيحه لكل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid says prayer belongs to human beings and glorification to all other creatures.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: الصلاة للبشر والتسبيح لما عداهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading changes “they do” to second-person address, adding warning and threat.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وعيسى وسلام وهارون عن أبي عمر وتفعلون بتاء الخطاب، وفيه وعيد وتخويف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All created things are under God's sovereign dominion, subject to His overpowering control; their return is to His reward or punishment, a reminder and warning.
rows.anchor: ولله ملك السماوات والأرض إخبار بأن جميع المخلوقات تحت ملكه يتصرف فيهم بما يشاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cloud and rain imagery follows the return to God as evidence of His control in changing states and anticipating resurrection; yuzjī means to drive gently and gradually, as with a heavy cloud or camel.
rows.anchor: ومعنى يزجي يسوق قليلا قليلا ويستعمل في سوق الثقيل برفق كالسحاب والإبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cloud is a collective noun; God moves one cloud toward another, joins their parts, and piles them densely so rain emerges through gaps formed by their compression.
rows.anchor: ثم يؤلف بينه أي بين أجزائه لأنه سحابة تتصل بسحابة

rows.speaker: ورش
rows.claim: Warsh reads “yuʾallif” with wāw; the other seven readers use hamza.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ورش يولف بالواو، وباقي السبعة بالهمز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Khilāl” is explained either as a singular or as a plural of khalal; Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and others read the singular “khalal.”
rows.anchor: والخلال: قيل مفرد. وقيل: جمع خلل كجبال وجبل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: The apparent meaning, held by Mujāhid, al-Kalbī, and most commentators, is that there are mountains of hail in the sky like mountains of stone on earth; others take “mountains” as a metaphor for abundance or an ellipsis of comparison.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن في السماء جبالا من برد قاله مجاهد والكلبي وأكثر المفسرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥūfī's appositional parse of the second “min” as referring to the sky fails: if it replaces the first, both must mark origin, as in “from Baghdad, from al-Karkh.”
rows.anchor: وهذا خطأ لأن الأولى لابتداء الغاية في ما دخلت عليه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya take the second “min” as partitive and the last as explanatory, so hail is the thing sent down from some sky-mountains.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري وابن عطية: هي للتبعيض فيكون على قولهما في موضع المفعول لينزل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī also allows the first two “min” particles to indicate origin and the final one to be partitive, making hail descend from mountains in the sky.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: أو الأولان للابتداء والأخيرة للتبعيض

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash treats the second and third “min” particles as redundant, with “mountains containing hail” as the direct object; al-Farrāʾ similarly says hail gathers like mountains for dramatic effect.
rows.anchor: وقيل: من الثانية والثالثة زائدتان وقاله الأخفش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another parse makes the first two “min” particles indicate origin and the third redundant, yielding hail from the mountains of the sky.
rows.anchor: وقيل: من الأولى والثانية لابتداء الغاية، والثالثة زائدة

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj compares the construction to an iron ring in one's hand: “of hail” qualifies the mountains and the object sent down is from those mountains, which must therefore be made of hail.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: معناه وينزل من السماء من جبال برد فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “with it” apparently refers to hail, but may refer to rain and hail together; rain more commonly brings harm, while diverting hail is a greater benefit and favor.
rows.anchor: والظاهر إعادة الضمير في به على البرد، ويحتمل أن يكون أريد به الودق والبرد

rows.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف
rows.claim: The usual reading is short “sanā” with singular “barq”; Ṭalḥa reads long “sanāʾ” and plural “buruq,” with another form harmonizing the two vowel marks. “Sanāʾ” means elevation or rank.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور سنا مقصورا برقه مفردا. وقرأ طلحة بن مصرف سناء ممدودا برقه

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar reads “yudhhib” passively; al-Akhfash and Abū Ḥātim criticize it, but the author defends it as transmitted and notes that Shayba also reads it so.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور يذهب بفتح الياء والهاء وأبو جعفر يذهب بضم الياء وكسر الهاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive reading is parsed either with an added bāʾ or with bāʾ meaning “from” and an omitted object, “removes the light from eyes”; a verse supports the latter usage.
rows.anchor: وخرج ذلك على زيادة الباء أي يذهب الأبصار. وعلى أن الباء بمعنى من

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night and day alternate, increase or diminish in length, change as clouds obscure sunlight or moonlight strengthens darkness, or differ in the benefits, harms, blessings, and trials apportioned in them.
rows.anchor: وتقليب الليل والنهار آيتان أحدهما بعد الآخر أو زيادة هذا وعكسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In that” points to the prior signs: glorification, clouds, rainfall and apportioned mercy, lightning, and the alternation of night and day; people of insight take these as admonition because sight and understanding disclose truth.
rows.anchor: إن في ذلك إشارة إلى ما تقدم من الدلائل الدالة على وحدانيته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read “khalaqa” as a past verb with “kulla” accusative; Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Ibn Waththāb, and al-Aʿmash read the active participle “khāliq” in construct with “every.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور خلق فعلا ماضيا. كل نصب. وقرأ حمزة والكسائي وابن وثاب والأعمش خالق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dābbah means any moving creature, including birds; a poem and a report about a sea animal exemplify the word. The inclusive “every creature” lets the rational-relative “man” cover nonrational beings too.
rows.anchor: والدابة: ما يحرك أمامه قدما ويدخل فيه الطير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent syntax makes “from water” the origin of creation; since most animals come from semen or depend on water, “every” may mean the predominant case, excluding angels from light, jinn from fire, Adam from earth, and Jesus from spirit.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن من ماء متعلق بخلق. ومن لابتداء الغاية، أي ابتداء خلقها من الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes all creatures universally and says water is the origin of all creation; a report says God first created a jewel that became water, from which fire, air, and light were made.
rows.anchor: وقيل كل دابة على العموم في هذه الأشياء كلها وإن أصل جميع المخلوقات الماء

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffāl instead makes “from water” an adjective of every creature, meaning each is generated from water and created by God.
rows.anchor: وقال القفال: ليس من ماء متعلقا بخلق وإنما هو في موضع الصفة لكل دابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Water” is indefinite here because it means the kind particular to each creature, perhaps semen; in 21:30 it is definite because the point is the common source of all animal kinds, even through intermediaries, like crops varied by one water.
rows.anchor: ونكر الماء هنا وعرف في وجعلنا من الماء كل شيء حي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Crawling on the belly is called walking by analogy with the following walkers or metaphorically, as Arabic calls events walking; it includes snakes, fish, worms, and similar creatures.
rows.anchor: وسمي الزحف على البطن مشيا لمشاكلته ما بعده من ذكر الماشين أو استعارة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two-legged walkers are humans and birds; four-legged walkers are other land animals. Creatures with more legs rely on only four when walking.
rows.anchor: وعلى رجلين الإنسان والطير والأربع لسائر حيوان الأرض من البهائم وغيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The list starts with the most astonishing sign, movement without walking limbs, followed by two legs and then four.
rows.anchor: وقدم ما هو أعرف في القدرة وأعجب وهو الماشي بغير آلة مشي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ubayy's codex adds “some walk on more,” but this is not established as Qurʾān; it may be an explanatory note about rare spiders, scorpions, tarantulas, and centipedes.
rows.anchor: وفي مصحف أبي ومنهم من يمشي على أكثر، فعم بهذه الزيادة جميع الحيوان لكنه لم يثبت قرآنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “God creates what He wills” means He originates whatever His will selects, underscoring both animal variety and differences beyond modes of locomotion.
rows.anchor: يخلق الله ما يشاء إشارة إلى أنه تعالى ما تعلقت به إرادة خلقه أنشأه واخترعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse responds to Quraysh treating the name al-Raḥmān as unknown by listing attributes that reveal and establish God's divinity; after creation of the heavens and mention of al-Raḥmān, they should worship Him rather than merely track celestial bodies.
rows.anchor: لما جعلت قريش سؤالها عن اسمه الذي هو الرحمن سؤالا عن مجهول نزلت هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent “constellations” are the twelve zodiac stations of the planets; their forms resemble what they are named for, and they are like high palaces or dwellings for their planets. The root suggests visibility.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن المراد بالبروج المعروفة عند العرب وهي منازل الكواكب السيارة

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash says the constellations are palaces in Paradise and reports that ʿAbd Allāh's companions read “palaces in heaven”; Abū Ṣāliḥ says they are great stars. Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects the Paradise reading as weakening the verse's appeal to observable evidence.
rows.anchor: وقيل: البروج هنا القصور في الجنة. قال الأعمش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “in it” apparently refers to the sky, though it may refer to the constellations as the setting containing a lamp.
rows.anchor: والضمير في فيها الظاهر أنه عائد على السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read singular “sirāj,” the sun; ʿAbd Allāh, ʿAlqama, al-Aʿmash, and the Kūfans read plural “suruj,” collective lights, thereby honoring the moon with separate mention.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور سراجا على الإفراد وهو الشمس. وقرأ عبد الله وعلقمة والأعمش والأخوان سرجا بالجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some read “qamar” with qāf ḍamma as a dialect form for moon; another takes it as the plural of moonlit night, with an omitted “night” retained in the adjective, as in Ḥassān's ellipsis for the water of Baradā.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن والأعمش والنخعي وعصمة عن عاصم وقمرا بضم إلقاء وسكون الميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The moon is called illuminating, not a lamp like the sun, because it is not self-igniting.
rows.anchor: ولم يجعله سراجا كالشمس لأنه لا توقد له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khilfah is parsed as a verbal noun or a noun of state used circumstantially: night and day each succeed and follow the other; Arabic also uses it for frequent back-and-forth, as in cited poetry.
rows.anchor: وانتصب خلفة على الحال. فقيل: هو مصدر خلف خلفة. وقيل: هو اسم هيئة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another gloss makes khilfah mean increase and decrease; Mujāhid, Qatāda, and al-Kisāʾī describe alternating darkness and brightness or long and short days.
rows.anchor: وقيل خلفة في الزيادة والنقصان. وقال مجاهد وقتادة والكسائي: هذا أسود وهذا أبيض

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, and al-Ḥasan say that anyone who misses good or prayer in one part of the cycle can make it up in the next.
rows.anchor: قال عمر وابن عباس والحسن: معناه لمن أراد أن يذكر ما فاته من الخير والصلاة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid and others understand remembrance as reflecting on created things and thanking God for intellect and understanding.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد وغيره: أي يعتبر بالمصنوعات ويشكر الله تعالى على نعمه عليه في العقل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī reports Ubayy b. Kaʿb's “yadhdhakkara” reading and says night and day reveal a powerful changer; rest at night and activity by day are blessings and opportunities to make up missed worship, as 28:73 explains.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: وعن أبي بن كعب يتذكر والمعنى

rows.speaker: النخعي
rows.claim: Al-Nakhaʿī, Ibn Waththāb, Zayd b. ʿAlī, Ṭalḥa, and Ḥamza read “tadhakkara” with the light form of the verb.
rows.anchor: وقرأ النخعي وابن وثاب وزيد بن علي وطلحة وحمزة تذكر مضارع ذكر خفيفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After condemning disbelievers, the passage turns to the remembering and grateful worshippers, calling them “servants of the Most Merciful” as an honorific title.
rows.anchor: جاء لمن أراد أن يذكر أو أراد شكورا ذكر أحوال المؤمنين المتذكرين الشاكرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAbd can mean servant or worshipper; Ibn Baḥr takes the plural as worshippers, while other explanations connect the historical name ʿIbād to Kisrā's control of ʿAbd al-Qays or their Christianity at al-Ḥīra. Readings vary between “ʿibād,” “ʿubud,” and a passive verb for walking.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن بحر: جمع عابد كصاحب وصحاب، وتاجر وتجار، وراجل ورجال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hawn means gentleness and softness; it describes unhurried, calm, graceful conduct without stamping or swagger, whether construed as a manner of walking or a circumstantial quality.
rows.anchor: والهون: الرفق واللين. وانتصب هونا على أنه نعت لمصدر محذوف

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid glosses gentle conduct as patience and dignity; Ibn ʿAbbās says obedience, chastity, and humility; al-Ḥasan says they remain forbearing when insulted.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: بالحلم والوقار. وقال ابن عباس: بالطاعة والعفاف والتواضع

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya takes hawn broadly as their way of life and social conduct; he rejects limiting it to gait alone, since even a criminal may walk softly, and connects their character to their manner.
rows.anchor: وإما أن يكون المراد صفة المشي وحده فباطل، لأن رب ماش هونا رويدا وهو ذنب أطلس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baytūtah means the night overtakes someone whether or not he sleeps; after their daytime conduct, the passage describes their night worship, apparently spending the night or most of it in prayer. Other views include any Qurʾān recitation in night prayer, two post-sunset or post-nightfall units, or witr after night prayer.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه يعني إحياء الليل بالصلاة أو أكثره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse encourages night prayer; prostration precedes standing in the wording for rhyme and because prostration is the servant's closest state to God. Abū al-Barhasam reads “sujūdan” on the pattern of “quʿūdan.”
rows.anchor: وفي هذه الآية حض على قيام الليل في الصلاة. وقدم السجود وإن كان متأخرا في الفعل لأجل الفواصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their prayer for protection from Hell confirms their belief in resurrection and recompense.
rows.anchor: ومدحهم تعالى بدعائه أن يصرف عنهم عذاب جهنم وفيه تحقيق إيمانهم بالبعث والجزاء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says gharām is dreadful and painful; al-Khudrī says clinging and enduring; al-Ḥasan compares Hell to a creditor from whom one cannot escape; al-Suddī says severe. Poetry by Bishr b. Abī Ḥātim and al-Aʿshā supports “inescapable.”
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: غراما فظيعا وجيعا. وقال الخدري: لازما ملحا دائما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning the prayer after night worship shows that, despite strenuous devotion, they remain fearful and implore God to spare them punishment.
rows.anchor: ثم عقبه بذكر دعائهم هذا إيذانا بأنهم مع اجتهادهم خائفون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “It is a bad resting place and abode” may use sāʾat as “how wretched,” with an omitted object of blame and “resting place and abode” as specification; or it may mean “grieves them,” with Hell as subject and the nouns as specifications or circumstantial phrases.
rows.anchor: وساءت احتمل أن يكون بمعنى بئست

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two descriptions are apparently distinct: enduring punishment and the misery of its place, though another view treats them as equivalent. The words apparently continue the supplicants' speech.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن التعليلين غير مترادفين ذكر أولا لزوم عذابها، وثانيا مساءة مكانها
